newsitem.title: USA: U.S. slams Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia on rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. slams Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia on rights.

text.p: Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia all committed human rights abuses last year, especially of ethnic minorities, the U.S. State Department said in its annual human rights report published on Thursday.

In Serbia, the government's rights record "continued to be poor," in Croatia it "remained poor," and in both parts of Bosnia the situation "remained precarious" as a result of abuses by the authorities, the worldwide report said.

The report charged that in Serbia the Socialist government had manipulated the courts to annul opposition victories in local elections in November, a move that has led to daily opposition demonstrations on the streets of Belgrade.
As a result, it said, "citizens cannot exercise their right to change their government".

It also said the Serbian police, controlled by President Slobodan Milosevic, had "committed extensive and systematic human rights abuses" including extrajudicial killings, torture, brutal beatings and arbitrary arrests.
Repression was directed particularly against Albanians in Kosovo and Moslems in Sandzak, it said, citing a report that authorities killed 14 ethnic Albanians in 1996.
In Croatia, the survey said, the government "continued to commit or allow serious abuses," especially of ethnic Serbs from rebel areas that were recaptured by Zagreb.
The government allowed only several thousand of approximately 180,000 Serbs who fled Croatian military action in 1995 to return in 1996, it said.
It also infringed on press freedom by cracking down on media that criticised it, the State Department said.
In Bosnia, the report criticised both the Moslem-Croat Federation and the Serb Republic, the two ethnically-based entities created by the 1995 Dayton peace accord.
Law enforcement bodies in both areas had given preferential treatment on the basis of political, ethnic and religious criteria, it said.

"To varying degrees the authorities in both (entities) continued to commit abuses, and the human rights situation remained precarious nearly a year after the signing of the peace agreement," the report said.
Despite the negative tone of the report, Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, who oversaw its publication, said he saw encouraging signs in both Bosnia and Serbia.
Bosnia, he said, had staged elections in September and was "beginning to put in place the building blocks of civil institutions" following its 43-month war.
In Serbia, Shattuck told a news conference, people were now expressing their desire for "democratic institutions in an open political system".
